summary: Round 1, test lane, on a decomposition with no code and no tests: the reviewable object is the TESTABILITY the three rows prescribe. What I verified as TRUE, against the tree rather than the prose: (a) ADR-0033 really does record the swap hazard M4.10c cites, in its own words -- 'nextOffset and oldestRetainedOffset are both uvarints in adjacent positions, so swapping them in encode AND decode round-trips by construction... Only a byte-level golden with distinct non-default values in both fields discriminates' -- and the existing GoldenCheckpointTest.java:60-65 already practises exactly that (1001/100 and 6006/600), so the prescription is the right remedy for the hazard it names; (b) CheckpointWriterContentTest exists and asserts what M4.10c claims -- theFirstCheckpointAfterATakeoverCarriesNoPodsAtAll at CheckpointWriterContentTest.java:130-157 drives a real takeover and asserts doesNotContainKey("poda"), and CheckpointWriter.java's javadoc carries the matching 'known hole' paragraph; (c) M4.10b's decision-only shape is PRECEDENTED and acceptable -- 61a335e (M4.3l) landed ADR-0031 as one file, 172 insertions, no production code and no tests, so check-tdd has nothing to see and that is not a defect. I did NOT find the M4.24/M4.27 'criterion that cannot fail' pattern stated outright in any row; what I did find is three criteria whose prescribed test admits a wrong implementation, named below with the surviving mutation for each. The strongest is M4.10d: its discriminator covers the sequencer takeover and NOT the pod restart, which is the failure the whole task is motivated by.

findings.title: M4.10d's discriminator covers a SEQUENCER takeover and not a POD restart, so the mutation the whole task exists to prevent survives it
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION: implement the dedup on the bare (podId, flushSeq), ignoring whatever M4.10b makes the key durable with. Walk the prescribed test: leader A applies poda#42; takeover; the successor recovers the window from the chain (M4.10c) and holds poda->42; poda replays 42 and is refused. The bare-pair mutant passes that unchanged -- the fixture contains exactly one incarnation of poda, so the durable component never varies and never discriminates. The scenario that kills the mutant is a POD restart, not a leader change: poda applies flushSeq 0,1,2, the process dies, comes back and issues 0 again for an ENTIRELY NEW segment, and the correct answer is ACCEPT. Under the mutant that genuine commit is SUPPRESSED -- which is verbatim the harm the M4.10 notes call 'worse than the duplication it exists to prevent' (backlog-notes.md:182-184) and the harm M4.10b's own row is written to avert (backlog.md:123). No row prescribes a test for it. The cross-leader-change discriminator is necessary and it is NOT sufficient; both must be named. Two further mutations M4.10d should also have to kill, neither named: (1) `flushSeq < lastApplied` in place of `<=` -- the EXACT-EQUAL replay is the actual retry case, and a fixture in this tree's existing habit (CheckpointWriterContentTest.java:118-128 replays 9 then 4, strictly lower) would not touch the boundary; (2) a single fleet-wide `long lastAppliedFlushSeq` in place of the per-pod map -- survives any single-pod workload and suppresses a second pod's genuine commit whose flushSeq happens to be lower. Remedy: state all three in M4.10d, and require M4.10b's ADR Consequences to name the pod-restart scenario as the thing M4.10d's test must kill -- that is what makes a decision-only commit falsifiable by the commit that implements it.

findings.title: 'Refuse a replayed pair' specifies the chain effect and says nothing about what the RETRYING CALLER gets back, and the obvious reading breaks the producer
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION: implement 'refuse' as skip-and-return -- the replayed request contributes no runs, and the returned CommitDelta simply does not carry the replayed segment key. Every criterion the three rows state stays green: no second set of offsets is assigned, the chain gains no second delta, lastAppliedFlushSeq is unchanged. But sequencer/src/main/java/binjava/sequencer/Sequencer.java:80-90 defines the return as the delta a caller finds ITS offsets in, matched on the segment key it submitted, and ingest/src/main/java/binjava/ingest/DefaultIngest.java:352-359 completes the append EXCEPTIONALLY with 'the commit did not carry the stream this append wrote' when the run is absent. So under that mutant a retry after an ambiguous IOException -- the exact case Sequencer.java:41-51 says M4.10 exists to make safe -- turns a flush that DID land into a producer-visible failure. The idempotency contract's whole point is that the second call is indistinguishable from the first, and none of b/c/d states that as a criterion. Remedy: M4.10d must prescribe the positive assertion -- a refused replay RETURNS the original offsets for the replayed segment key, byte-equal to what the first attempt returned -- not merely that the chain did not grow.

findings.title: Every criterion M4.10c states is format-level, so a delta that carries the field and never populates it lands green -- and the one end-to-end anchor the row cites is left as a negative assertion under pressure to be deleted
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION: add per-pod flushSeq to the record and the codec, bump the version, update every reader, writer and fake, commit chain-delta-v2.bin -- and have CommitLog.commitAll construct the delta with an empty (or all-zero) pod map. The version, the readers, the writers, the fakes and the new golden are all green, because the golden fixture is HAND-BUILT in the test and never travels the commit path: GoldenCheckpointTest.java:25-35 records precisely this limit about itself, measured ('nothing in this class builds a fixture -- it reads committed bytes'). The row's stated deliverables are all satisfied and a new leader still recovers an empty window, which is the hole M4.10c exists to close. The anchor that WOULD kill it already exists and the row half-points at it: CheckpointWriterContentTest.java:130-157 asserts doesNotContainKey("poda") after a real takeover, and that assertion becomes FALSE the moment M4.10c works. As written -- 'asserts the empty-pods case deliberately, to make this task confront it' -- 'confront' is equally satisfiable by DELETING or loosening that assertion, which is the testing.md rule 5 / check-test-integrity.sh inversion (a production change landing beside a weakened assertion). Remedy: prescribe the replacement explicitly -- that test is INVERTED to assert the successor's first checkpoint carries poda -> 42, recovered from the chain -- so M4.10c has one criterion that fails against a field nothing populates.

findings.title: The golden prescription takes ADR-0033's swap lesson and drops its ORDER lesson, which the same ADR's golden was measured NOT to carry
findings.failure_scenario: The citation is accurate and 'distinct non-default values in every field' is the right remedy for the swap. But ADR-0033's golden carries a second, separately measured limitation, written into GoldenCheckpointTest.java:25-29: 'both delete-the-sort mutations leave all three tests here GREEN, because nothing in this class builds a fixture -- it reads committed bytes.' SURVIVING MUTATION, if per-pod flushSeq is encoded as a keyed collection: delete the canonical ordering in CommitDelta.encode. The golden still decodes, its values still assert, and re-encode is still byte-identical -- decode preserves the file's order, so the fixture can never detect that a FRESHLY BUILT record would encode differently. ADR-0033's 'two checkpoints carrying the same facts encode identically' property then silently stops holding for deltas. Remedy: prescribe the companion order test on a freshly built record (what CheckpointTest is to GoldenCheckpointTest), OR state that the field rides on SegmentCommit as a scalar rather than as a map -- the shape decides whether the second test is owed, and the row does not say which shape it means.

findings.title: No production caller ever replays a pair, so the parent row's stated harm has no end-to-end test that could fail against any of b/c/d
findings.failure_scenario: The parent row's harm is 'a retried pod is assigned offsets twice'. ingest/src/main/java/binjava/ingest/DefaultIngest.java:349 is the ONLY issuance site in production and it evaluates `flushSeq++` in the argument list on every attempt, success or failure; the catch at the end of flushLocked fails the batch and never re-sends. So no production path today ever re-submits a (podId, flushSeq), and every M4.10d test is necessarily a synthetic caller re-invoking the seam by hand. That is the M4.7c shape this backlog already records against itself -- 'built BatchingSequencer and nothing constructs one outside its own test' -- and it means the criterion a reader takes from the parent row is one nothing can fail. Remedy: name the retry-with-the-same-pair caller as explicitly out of scope for b/c/d (a row of its own), rather than leaving it implied by the parent.

findings.title: M4.10c's fifth golden falsifies a census sentence the row does not mention
findings.failure_scenario: That javadoc opens 'FOUR FILES -- one per shape, and TWO for a delta', and chain-delta-v2.bin makes it five. It cannot go red -- it is a comment -- so it just becomes false, which is the stale-inventory shape the M4.9 archive row diagnoses at length ('a sentence counting assertions elsewhere is false as soon as any of them moves, and the commit moving them is usually this one'). One clause in M4.10c naming it as a site to edit costs nothing now and is missed later.
